title: GATE CS Topic Test — Computer Networks (Set 2)
titleEn: GATE CS Topic Test — Computer Networks (Set 2)

questions.questionTextEn: The 'count-to-infinity' problem (slow convergence after a link failure) is a classic drawback of:
questions.explanationEn: In Distance Vector routing, routers only know next-hop distances without full path visibility, so routing loops can form after a link goes down until hop counts slowly increment to infinity.

questions.questionTextEn: In a fully connected point-to-point mesh network of 10 routers, how many duplex links are required?
questions.explanationEn: A complete graph `K_n` has `n(n - 1) / 2 = 10 × 9 / 2 = 45` links.

questions.questionTextEn: How many usable host IPv4 addresses are available in a `/27` subnet (excluding network and broadcast addresses)?
questions.explanationEn: Host bits = `32 - 27 = 5`. Usable hosts = `2^5 - 2 = 32 - 2 = 30`.

questions.questionTextEn: A packet of size 1500 bytes is transmitted over a 12 Mbps (`12 × 10^6` bits/s) link. What is the transmission delay in milliseconds?
Consider the CIDR block `192.168.10.0/26`. Which of the following statements are TRUE?
optionsEn: The block contains 64 total IPv4 addresses and 62 usable host addresses
The broadcast address of this subnet is `192.168.10.63`
The IP address `192.168.10.65` belongs to this subnet
questions.explanationEn: `/26` leaves 6 host bits (`2^6 = 64` addresses: `.0` network, `.1`–`.62` usable hosts, `.63` broadcast; mask `.192`). `.65` belongs to the next `/26` subnet (`192.168.10.64/26`), so D is false.

questions.questionTextEn: In Selective Repeat ARQ with `k`-bit sequence numbers, what is the maximum allowable sender window size `W_s` (assuming `W_s = W_r`)?
questions.explanationEn: Selective Repeat requires `W_s + W_r <= 2^k`. With equal sender and receiver windows (`W_s = W_r`), `W_s <= 2^(k-1)`.

questions.questionTextEn: To GUARANTEE detection of up to `d` single-bit errors in a block code, what must be the minimum Hamming distance `d_min` between any two valid codewords?
questions.explanationEn: Detecting up to `d` bit errors requires `d_min >= d + 1` (so flipping up to `d` bits can never turn one valid codeword into another). Correcting `t` errors requires `d_min >= 2t + 1`.

questions.questionTextEn: What is the maximum theoretical channel throughput (efficiency) of Slotted ALOHA compared to Pure ALOHA?
questions.explanationEn: Slotted ALOHA halves the vulnerable time period from `2T_fr` to `T_fr`, doubling maximum throughput from `1/(2e) ≈ 18.4%` to `1/e ≈ 36.8%`.

questions.questionTextEn: If the payload bit stream `011111111110` (ten consecutive `1`s between two `0`s) is processed by standard HDLC bit stuffing, how many `0` bits are inserted into the stream?
questions.explanationEn: A `0` is inserted after the first five `1`s, and another `0` is inserted after the next five `1`s (`011111[0]11111[0]0`), inserting 2 bits.

questions.questionTextEn: Standard DNS queries typically use which transport-layer protocol and well-known port number?
questions.explanationEn: Standard DNS lookups use lightweight UDP port 53 for low-latency request-response (falling back to TCP port 53 for zone transfers or responses exceeding UDP size limits).

questions.topicTag: CN — Minimum Packet Count in Fragmentation
questions.questionTextEn: An application sends a 5000-byte UDP message (8-byte UDP header) over IPv4 (20-byte IP header) across a link with MTU = 1020 bytes. How many IPv4 fragments are sent?
questions.explanationEn: IPv4 payload = `5000 + 8 = 5008` bytes. Max IPv4 payload per fragment = `floor((1020 - 20) / 8) * 8 = 1000` bytes. Fragments = `ceil(5008 / 1000) = 6`.

questions.topicTag: CN — HTTP Objects with Parallel Connections
questions.questionTextEn: A web page has 1 base HTML file and 8 images. Using non-persistent HTTP/1.0 with up to 4 parallel TCP connections at a time (ignoring transmission time), how many total RTTs are needed to download the base HTML file and all 8 images?
questions.explanationEn: Base HTML takes 2 RTTs (1 TCP + 1 HTTP). Then 4 images are fetched in parallel (2 RTTs), followed by the remaining 4 images in parallel (2 RTTs). Total = `2 + 2 + 2 = 6 RTTs`.

questions.questionTextEn: In a TCP 3-way handshake, Client sends `SYN` with `Seq = 500`. Server replies with `SYN+ACK` with `Seq = 2000`. What are the `Ack` number in the Server's `SYN+ACK` and the `(Seq, Ack)` in the Client's final `ACK` (assuming no data payload)?
questions.explanationEn: Both `SYN` flags consume 1 phantom sequence number. Thus Server acknowledges `500 + 1 = 501`, and Client sends its final ACK with `Seq = 501` and `Ack = 2000 + 1 = 2001`.

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following statements comparing intra-AS and inter-AS routing protocols are TRUE?
optionsEn: BGP prevents routing loops by advertising the full AS-PATH attribute
OSPF is an intra-AS link-state protocol that runs directly over IP (protocol 89)
BGP is an inter-AS path-vector protocol that runs over TCP (port 179)
RIP uses hop count as its metric with a maximum valid path length of 15 hops
questions.explanationEn: All four statements are accurate technical facts about OSPF, RIP, and BGP.

questions.questionTextEn: A sender uses Go-Back-N with window size `W = 4` to send 10 frames (numbered 1 through 10). Suppose ONLY frame 4 is lost on its first transmission (all other frames and ACKs arrive safely). How many TOTAL frame transmissions are required to deliver all 10 frames?
questions.explanationEn: Frames 1, 2, 3 succeed. Frame 4 is lost, and before timing out the sender transmits the rest of its window (frames 5, 6, 7), which the receiver discards. Upon timeout, Go-Back-N retransmits frames 4, 5, 6, 7 and then sends 8, 9, 10. Total transmissions = 10 + 4 = 14.

questions.questionTextEn: In TCP, the `Data Offset` (header length) field is 4 bits wide and counts 32-bit words. What is the MAXIMUM possible size of a TCP header (including options) in bytes?
questions.explanationEn: Maximum 4-bit value is `15`. `15 × 4 bytes = 60` bytes (20-byte fixed header + up to 40 bytes of options).

questions.questionTextEn: Two stations A and B collide for the 1st time on an Ethernet LAN and both run Binary Exponential Backoff (`k ∈ {0, 1}`). What is the probability that they collide AGAIN on their very next attempt?
questions.explanationEn: Each station independently picks `0` or `1` with probability `1/2`. They collide again iff both pick `0` (`1/4`) or both pick `1` (`1/4`), giving `1/4 + 1/4 = 0.50`.

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following mechanisms help mitigate congestion or improve throughput in IP/TCP networks?
optionsEn: Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease (AIMD) in TCP Congestion Avoidance
Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) bits in IP and TCP headers
Random Early Detection (RED) active queue management at routers
Disabling all checksums in Ethernet frames
questions.explanationEn: AIMD, ECN, and RED are standard congestion-control techniques. Disabling checksums undermines error detection and does not address congestion (D is false).

questions.questionTextEn: In legacy classful IPv4 addressing, how many usable host addresses exist in a single Class C network (`/24`)?
questions.explanationEn: A Class C network has 8 host bits, yielding `2^8 - 2 = 254` usable host addresses.

questions.questionTextEn: TCP estimates `EstimatedRTT` using `EstimatedRTT = (1 - α) * EstimatedRTT + α * SampleRTT` with `α = 0.25`. If the current `EstimatedRTT` is 100 ms and a new `SampleRTT` of 140 ms is measured, what is the updated `EstimatedRTT`?
